```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
orange = data.frame(Orange)
```

# Repeated Measures

::: {.callout-note title="Learning Goals" collapse="false"}
After this lesson, you should be able to:

* Explain what partial pooling is
* Explain why partial pooling is useful
* Use R to fit a hierarchical model with a partially pooled intercept
:::

:::{.callout-important title="Required Packages"}
This chapter uses the following R packages:

* ggplot2
* lme4

For a refresher about how to install and load packages, see the
[Packages][r-basics-packages] section of DataLab's R Basics workshop reader.

[r-basics-packages]: https://ucdavisdatalab.github.io/dwr_workshop_r_basics/chapters/getting-started/getting-started.html#sec-packages
:::

This chapter introduces **hierarchical models**, multi-part linear models which
are a fundamental tool for modeling repeated measures data. Along the way, we
explain a few of the ideas that underpin these models.


## Partial Pooling

Datasets often contain features that we can use to group the observations. For
instance, a dataset where the subjects are people might include features such
as city of residence, educational attainment, and marriage status. If one of
these features (or one of the subpopulations they characterize) is important to
our analysis goals, we'll likely use the feature to group the observations
during analysis.

Repeated measures datasets present another case where there are features we can
use to group observations. Because the measurements for each subject are
repeated, we might want to group observations by subject (or by time of
measurement).

In the Orange Tree Growth dataset (@sec-dataset-orange), each tree has a unique
ID number. We can use this to plot the observations for each tree separately:

```{r}
#| label: fig-orange-facet
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Per-tree scatterplots of age versus circumference for the Orange Tree
#|    Growth dataset.
library("ggplot2")

ggplot(Orange) +
  aes(x = age, y = circumference) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ Tree)
```

If we want to compute a statistic on a dataset with groups, two strategies we
might consider are:

* Compute a separate estimate for each group. This is a **no pooling**
  strategy, because we never pool the groups.

* Compute one estimate, ignoring the groups. This is a **complete pooling**
  strategy, because we combine---or **pool**---all of the groups.

The no pooling strategy has the obvious advantage that it reveals details about
the groups that we would otherwise miss with the complete pooling strategy. On
the other hand, the complete pooling strategy also has an advantage: even if
the number observations in some groups is small, by pooling them we'll likely
have enough observations to get an accurate estimate.

As an extreme case, consider what happens if some of the groups have only one
observation. The estimates for these groups will likely be poor, because they
depend entirely on sampling of a single observations. As an even more extreme
case, if some groups are empty (no observations), then we can't compute an
estimate at all.

We can use a third strategy, **partial pooling**, to improve on the other two.
The idea is to compute the no pooling estimates (for groups with observations)
and the complete pooling estimate, then take the a weighted average (or linear
interpolation) of the two. The average is weighted with the sample size and
precision (inverse variance) of each estimate, so that:

* For groups with many observations and high precision, the average will be
  close to the no pooling estimate;
* For groups with few observations and low precision, the average will be close
  to the complete pooling estimate.

In other words, partial pooling shares information between groups, while still
providing a separate estimate for each one. It also allows us to compute
estimates for groups with only zero or one observation.

Partial pooling is useful when working with repeated measures datasets because
sometimes a measurement might be missing. It also leads to more accurate
estimates even when all of the observations are there.


## Hierarchical Models

We can reap the benefits of partial pooling in a linear modeling context by
using a **hierarchical model**. Hierarchical models are also known as
multilevel models and linear mixed effect models (LMMs). They're called
hierarchical models because partial pooling is equivalent to fitting a
hierarchy of models: one at the dataset level and one or more at the group
level.

As a brief demonstration of how to fit a hierarchical model, let's fit models
with no pooling, complete pooling, and partial pooling. We'll use the Orange
Tree Growth dataset, with circumference as the outcome and age as a predictor.
When we group the observations, we'll group by tree.

Let's start with the complete pooling strategy. We'll fit a single model,
ignoring the groups entirely:

```{r}
# Complete pooling:
fit_compl = lm(circumference ~ age, orange)
summary(fit_compl)
```

There's only one intercept in this model, computed based on all of the
observations.

Next, let's try the no pooling strategy. For this, we'll fit the model with a
separate intercept for each tree. To do so, we can add `-1` in the model
formula to remove the pooled intercept:

```{r}
# No pooling:
fit_no = lm(circumference ~ age + Tree - 1, orange)
summary(fit_no)
```

Finally, let's try the partial pooling strategy. The [lme4][] package is one of
several packages we can use to fit a hierarchical model in R. We'll use its
`lmer` function, which is a lot like the `lm` function. In the model formula,
we'll add the groups as `(1 | Tree)`. This is lme4's notation for partially
pooled intercept (another name for this is a **random effect**):

```{r}
# Partial pooling:
library("lme4")

fit_part = lmer(circumference ~ age + (1 | Tree) - 1, orange)
summary(fit_part)
```

The residual standard deviation for the partial pooling model is only slightly
higher than it is for the no pooling model, and we get the benefits of partial
pooling.

The example in this section only shows the simplest way to use a hierachical
model. There are many other ways to use them, such as computing partially
pooled slopes, that are useful for all kinds of grouped datasets.

:::{.callout-note title="See Also"}
The blog post [_Partial Pooling in Mixed-Effects Models_][partial] [@mahr2017]
gives a nice demonstration of partial pooling with visual examples.

DataLab's [A Practical Introduction to Regression Modeling in R][dl-reg-model]
workshop reader includes a longer introduction to hierarchical models.

The textbook _Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical
Models_ [@gelman2007] provides a thorough introduction to hierarchical models.

Hierarchical models are closely associated with Bayesian statistics; for an
introduction to Bayesian statistics, see the textbook _Statistical Rethinking_
[@mcelreath2020].

[partial]: https://www.tjmahr.com/plotting-partial-pooling-in-mixed-effects-models/
